lines.text: A kingdom high in the mountains, wholly surrounded by South Africa, founded by one wise king and kept free by its peaks. This is the story of Lesotho.
In the 1820s, as war scattered the peoples of southern Africa, Moshoeshoe gathered them together and founded the Basotho nation.
In 1824 he made the flat-topped mountain of Thaba Bosiu his stronghold, and from it he held off Boers and Zulus alike.
In 1869 a police camp was set up beside the Caledon River. It grew into Maseru, the capital.
To keep his land from the Boers, Moshoeshoe had asked for British protection. As Basutoland it stayed out of South Africa.
Leabua Jonathan would become the first prime minister, and in 1970 he seized full power.
Moshoeshoe the second was king at independence, and was twice sent into exile in the troubled years that followed.
His son, Letsie the third, born in 1963, has been king since 1996.
In 1966 Basutoland became the independent Kingdom of Lesotho, a mountain land ringed on every side by South Africa.
High in the mountains, Sehlabathebe became a national park in 1969, its rocks painted long ago by the San people.
And from 1986 great dams and tunnels began sending the mountains' water to Johannesburg, now one of Lesotho's main exports.
From Moshoeshoe's mountain to the water of its highlands, Lesotho's peaks still keep it.
